quests.instruction: A candidate is asked whether they can start next week.
quests.word: I should be able to start next week.
quests.textToSpeak: I should be able to start next week.
quests.hint: Does 'should' lift into doubt, or stay light before a firm landing?
quests.explanation: Keeping 'should' light and falling decisively on 'week' lets the speaker hedge out of courtesy while still sounding reliable. Doubt would stretch 'should' and lift towards the end, leaving the listener unsure. Both versions use identical words, so only the landing separates a safe hire from a risky one.
quests.meaningShift: A light 'should' with a firm landing is courteous but dependable; a stretched 'should' with a lift would show doubt.

quests.instruction: A colleague agrees to review your slides.
quests.word: Yeah, I can take a look at it.
quests.textToSpeak: Yeah, I can take a look at it.
quests.hint: Which of 'yeah' and 'can' sounds like it carries real energy?
quests.explanation: Brightness on 'yeah' and a loose fall on 'it' give the impression of someone with spare time and no resentment. Reluctance would flatten 'yeah' and press on 'can', as if the offer were being squeezed out. Listeners use this difference to decide whether to hand over the slides now or wait.
quests.meaningShift: A bright start and loose fall sound unhurried; a flat 'yeah' with a pressed 'can' would sound reluctant.

quests.instruction: A host asks whether you'd like tea. You would.
quests.word: Only if it's no trouble.
quests.textToSpeak: Only if it's no trouble.
quests.hint: Decide whether the voice settles, or stays hesitant on 'trouble'.
quests.explanation: Settling on 'trouble' after a soft, quick start shows the speaker is following the courtesy ritual of not seeming greedy. Genuine reluctance would lift on 'trouble' and slow down, inviting the host to withdraw the offer. Hosts depend on this to know whether to go ahead and make the tea.
quests.meaningShift: A settled fall is ritual politeness; a lifted, slowed ending would show real reluctance.

quests.instruction: A sales director is addressing the team at quarter-end.
quests.word: I'm confident we'll hit the target.
quests.textToSpeak: I'm confident we'll hit the target.
quests.hint: Is the force spread evenly, or all dumped on 'confident'?
quests.explanation: Measured force on 'confident' and a calm fall on 'target' sound like conclusions drawn from evidence. Bluster would push 'confident' hard, widen the range and speed up, as though volume could substitute for proof. Colleagues learn to hear that difference before trusting a forecast.
quests.modulationPattern: Measured peak on 'confident', calm fall on 'target'.
quests.meaningShift: Measured force sounds evidence-based; a hard, wide push on 'confident' would sound like bluster.

quests.instruction: A colleague is pitching an idea to a nervous client.
quests.word: Trust me, this will work.
quests.textToSpeak: Trust me, this will work.
quests.hint: Does the pace invite another question, or block it?
quests.explanation: Slowing on 'trust me' and falling gently on 'work' gives the client time to relax. Closing down questions would speed up, press 'will' and land hard, leaving no space to respond. Clients tend to ask more if the first version is used and fewer if the second is.
quests.meaningShift: A slow, gentle delivery reassures; a fast, pressed one with a hard landing would shut the discussion.

quests.instruction: An engineer is defending a new design in a meeting.
quests.word: There's no way that can fail.
quests.textToSpeak: There's no way that can fail.
quests.hint: Does 'no way' bounce, or hit down?
quests.explanation: Lifting and bouncing on 'no way' sounds like someone eager to show how robust the design is, with energy that invites others in. Dismissing concerns would flatten 'no way' and land heavily on 'fail', closing the conversation. Colleagues respond to this by either engaging or backing off.
quests.modulationPattern: Lifted, bouncing 'no way', light fall on 'fail'.
quests.meaningShift: A bouncing contour shows excitement; a flat, heavy one would dismiss the concerns.

quests.instruction: A colleague who never apologises is reported to have apologised.
quests.word: He actually said sorry to everyone?
quests.textToSpeak: He actually said sorry to everyone?
quests.hint: How high does 'actually' go, and does the rise stay wide?
quests.explanation: Lifting 'actually' high and rising widely on 'everyone' shows that the speaker accepts the news and is amazed by it. Doubt would keep the range narrower and press on 'said', as though testing the claim. Speakers choose one or the other depending on whether they believe it.
quests.meaningShift: A high 'actually' with a wide rise shows astonishment; a narrow rise with a pressed 'said' would test the claim.

quests.instruction: A manager says the deadline has been extended by a month.
quests.word: They're giving us the whole month?
quests.textToSpeak: They're giving us the whole month?
quests.hint: Notice whether the voice rises brightly, or tightens.
quests.explanation: Rising brightly and widely on 'month' conveys relief and delight, and no suspicion is audible. A wary speaker would tighten, slow down on 'whole' and lower the end of the rise. Hearing delight tells the manager the news has landed well.
quests.meaningShift: A bright, wide rise is delight; a tight, slow rise with weight on 'whole' would suggest suspicion.

quests.instruction: A colleague confesses the report was always going to be late.
quests.word: So the report was always going to be late?
quests.textToSpeak: So the report was always going to be late?
quests.hint: Check whether the voice sounds stunned, or sharp.
quests.explanation: Dropping on 'always' and rising slowly and softly shows the speaker is processing bad news. Accusation would be sharper, with weight on 'always' and a clipped rise. This helps the confessor decide between explaining and defending.
quests.meaningShift: A slow, soft rise with a drop on 'always' is dismay; a sharp, clipped one would accuse.

quests.instruction: A manager speaks to the team at the end of a project.
quests.word: Great work, everyone, really.
quests.textToSpeak: Great work, everyone, really.
quests.hint: What does the voice do on the final 'really'?
quests.explanation: Giving 'really' its own small fall and a warm tone adds a personal confirmation that the praise is not a formula. A routine version would run the whole phrase at one level and drop 'really' on to the end. Staff notice the difference, and it shapes how much they believe future praise.
quests.meaningShift: A separate, warm 'really' adds sincerity; an even, flat run-through would be routine.

quests.instruction: A recorded message plays while you wait on hold.
quests.word: We really do value your feedback.
quests.textToSpeak: We really do value your feedback.
quests.hint: Is any word pushed in a way that suggests a person thinking?
quests.explanation: Even weight on every word with a predictable fall on 'feedback' is typical of lines performed thousands of times. Genuine interest would show unevenness, perhaps lingering on 'value'. Most callers learn to hear the evenness as a sign of a script.
quests.modulationPattern: Even weight with a predictable fall on 'feedback'.
quests.meaningShift: Even, predictable delivery is a script; uneven, thoughtful delivery would show real interest.

quests.instruction: A host welcomes a friend who arrives late to a party.
quests.word: I'm so glad you could make it.
quests.textToSpeak: I'm so glad you could make it.
quests.hint: Does 'glad' stretch?
quests.explanation: Lengthening and lifting 'glad', then letting 'it' fall softly, makes the greeting sound like a response to this particular guest. An automatic reply would be quick, flat and identical for every arrival. Friends feel the first and politely note the second.
quests.meaningShift: A stretched, lifted 'glad' is personal; a quick, flat delivery is automatic.

quests.instruction: A colleague gets a small detail wrong in a meeting.
quests.word: Actually, it was on Thursday.
quests.textToSpeak: Actually, it was on Thursday.
quests.hint: Is the tone cushioned, or sharp?
quests.explanation: Softening 'actually' and settling on 'Thursday' provides the right day without making the colleague look foolish. Contradicting to win would stress 'actually' sharply and finish with an edge. This difference affects how the colleague reacts, whether gratefully or defensively.
quests.meaningShift: A soft opener and settled fall correct helpfully; a sharp opener and edged finish would contradict.

quests.instruction: A debate is going badly and one speaker cuts in.
quests.word: No, no, no, that's completely wrong.
quests.textToSpeak: No, no, no, that's completely wrong.
quests.hint: Judge whether the speaker offers anything in place of what was said.
quests.explanation: Three quick 'no's, heavy stress on 'completely' and a hard fall on 'wrong' shut the other person down without proposing a replacement. A helpful correction would offer the right information and soften the tone. In meetings, this is the difference between a debate and an argument.
quests.meaningShift: Heavy repeated rejection contradicts; a soft offer of the right information would correct.

quests.instruction: A colleague quietly steps in during a meeting.
quests.word: I think you'll find it's Thursday.
quests.textToSpeak: I think you'll find it's Thursday.
quests.hint: Is 'think' heavy, with a drawn-out 'find'?
quests.explanation: Dragging 'find' and putting dry weight on 'Thursday' gives the phrase a superior edge, as though the listener should have known. A friendly suggestion would stay light, with a lift on 'Thursday' that leaves room for doubt. People often hear the edge without being able to name it.
quests.meaningShift: A dry, drawn-out delivery sounds condescending; a light lift on 'Thursday' would be friendly.

quests.instruction: A manager has decided against your advice.
quests.word: Well, it's your call.
quests.textToSpeak: Well, it's your call.
quests.hint: Does 'your' carry weight?
quests.explanation: Weight on 'your' and a flat fall on 'call' put responsibility on the manager, and the speaker distances themselves. Happy delegation would be warmer and lighter, as an expression of trust. Hearing the distance tells you to expect little help if things go wrong.
quests.meaningShift: Weight on 'your' with a flat fall distances the speaker; a warm, light delivery would hand over trust.

quests.instruction: A meeting is choosing between time slots.
quests.word: Whatever works for everyone.
quests.textToSpeak: Whatever works for everyone.
quests.hint: Does the energy hold, or drain away on 'everyone'?
quests.explanation: Steady energy and a comfortable fall on 'everyone' suggest that no option bothers the speaker. Giving up would sag on 'works' and trail off, hinting the speaker would prefer not to be asked. It is easy to mistake one for the other without listening to how the sentence ends.
quests.meaningShift: A steady, comfortable fall is flexible; a sagging, trailing one is giving up.

quests.instruction: A friend plans to move abroad.
quests.word: I won't stand in your way.
quests.textToSpeak: I won't stand in your way.
quests.hint: How heavy is 'won't', and how slowly does it end?
quests.explanation: Lowering the pitch on 'won't' and falling slowly on 'way' leave room for the feeling the speaker is not stating. Full enthusiasm would lift and quicken. The sad version lets the friend know that support is real but it has a cost.
quests.meaningShift: A low, slow delivery is supportive but sad; a lifted, quick one would be enthusiastic.

quests.instruction: A manager reads out two agenda items.
quests.word: We need to talk about the budget and the schedule.
quests.textToSpeak: We need to talk about the budget and the schedule.
quests.hint: Compare the strength of the pitch on the two item names.
quests.explanation: Equal peaks on 'budget' and 'schedule' present them as two matching items, with a rise on the first and a fall on the second. If 'budget' dominated, 'schedule' would be reduced into a trailing tag. Staff use this to tell whether both topics will get equal time.
quests.meaningShift: Equal peaks treat both items as equals; a dominant 'budget' with a reduced 'schedule' would demote the second.

quests.instruction: A friend reviews a concert.
quests.word: It was a bit disappointing, really.
quests.textToSpeak: It was a bit disappointing, really.
quests.hint: How much does 'disappointing' stand out from its neighbours?
quests.explanation: Keeping the peak on 'disappointing' small, tempered by 'a bit' and 'really', lowers the temperature of the criticism. A strong peak would drop on the word and make the review sound harsh. Listeners decide whether the friend recommends or warns against it.
quests.modulationPattern: Small peak on 'disappointing', soft fall on 'really'.
quests.meaningShift: A small peak keeps the criticism mild; a strong peak would sound harsh.

quests.instruction: A colleague describes a tight schedule.
quests.word: I mean, it's not impossible.
quests.textToSpeak: I mean, it's not impossible.
options: Faint hope: 'impossible' has a small fall
quests.correctAnswer: Faint hope: 'impossible' has a small fall
quests.hint: Find the word that seems to be weighed most.
quests.explanation: Falling only slightly on 'impossible', with 'not' kept light, leaves a slim possibility on the table. A peak on 'not' would stress the denial and sound defensive, as if someone had claimed it was impossible. The hedge 'I mean' also suggests the speaker is thinking aloud.
quests.meaningShift: A small fall on 'impossible' signals faint hope; a peak on 'not' would stress that it can be done.

quests.instruction: A colleague has just said, 'The client wants it by Friday.'
quests.word: Friday. Right.
quests.textToSpeak: Friday. Right.
quests.hint: Which word comes after a pause, and how does it end?
quests.explanation: Pausing after 'Friday' and saying 'right' low and slow shows the speaker is working out the consequences. Calm acceptance would be quick and light. In context, the first version tells the colleague to expect pushback soon.
quests.meaningShift: A pause with a low, slow 'right' shows processing; a quick, light one would be calm.

quests.instruction: A colleague has plans tonight but a deadline is looming.
quests.word: It's fine, I'll just stay late.
quests.textToSpeak: It's fine, I'll just stay late.
quests.hint: Is 'fine' heavy, and does 'late' sink?
quests.explanation: Weighted 'fine' and a sinking 'late' show that the speaker is resigned and hoping someone will say 'no, don't'. A cheerful offer would be bright and quick throughout. The context of having plans makes the first reading more likely.
quests.meaningShift: A weighted 'fine' with a sinking 'late' invites a rescue; a bright, quick offer would be cheerful.

quests.instruction: A friend has delayed a decision about your shared plan.
quests.word: Okay, well, let me know.
quests.textToSpeak: Okay, well, let me know.
quests.hint: How much energy remains after 'well'?
quests.explanation: Saying 'well' low and letting 'know' fall flat shows that the speaker is making an effort to be patient. Relaxed flexibility would keep brightness through the sentence. It is a cue that the friend might want the decision sooner.
quests.meaningShift: A low, flat delivery is patient disappointment; a bright one would be relaxed.

quests.instruction: A guest hopes someone has a spare charger.
quests.word: I was just wondering whether you might possibly have a spare.
quests.textToSpeak: I was just wondering whether you might possibly have a spare.
quests.hint: Are all the hedging words equally gentle?
quests.explanation: Light, rising stresses on 'just', 'might' and 'possibly' pile softeners on top of one another, showing the speaker is eager not to impose. Sarcasm would flatten and exaggerate one or two of them. The listener should respond to the request, not to the politeness.
quests.modulationPattern: Light rising stress on each hedge.
quests.meaningShift: Evenly rising hedges soften the request; a flat, exaggerated one would be sarcastic.

quests.instruction: A guest is hesitant about opening a window.
quests.word: Would it be an awful nuisance if I opened the window?
quests.textToSpeak: Would it be an awful nuisance if I opened the window?
quests.hint: Is 'awful' sincere, or dripping?
quests.explanation: Rising gently and unevenly on 'awful' and 'window' shows the speaker is truly worried about inconveniencing others. Irony would stretch 'awful' and drop in a dry fall. The listener can relax and say yes if the first version is used.
quests.meaningShift: A gentle, uneven rise shows real concern; a stretched, dry delivery would be ironic.

quests.instruction: Someone is blocking your path in a corridor.
quests.word: I don't mean to be rude, but you're in my way.
quests.textToSpeak: I don't mean to be rude, but you're in my way.
quests.hint: Spot which half has the weight.
quests.explanation: Weight on 'my' and a firm fall on 'way' reveal that the real message is the complaint, with the opening serving as a cushion. An apologetic version would lift on 'way' and soften. This helps the listener move without arguing.
quests.modulationPattern: Light opener, weight on 'my', firm fall on 'way'.
quests.meaningShift: A light opener and a firm second half is cushioned annoyance; a softened lift would be apologetic.

quests.instruction: A colleague has just called your design 'a mess'.
quests.word: I wouldn't put it quite like that.
quests.textToSpeak: I wouldn't put it quite like that.
quests.hint: Which word gets the main push, and how does the end fall?
quests.explanation: Weight on 'wouldn't' and 'quite', with a firm fall on 'that', shows a polite but clear rejection of the label. Agreeing with edits would lift on 'that' and sound open. The distinction tells the colleague whether the argument is over.
quests.modulationPattern: Weight on 'wouldn't' and 'quite', firm fall on 'that'.
quests.meaningShift: Weighted negation with a firm fall disagrees diplomatically; a lift on 'that' would invite edits.

quests.instruction: A manager hears a suggestion in a meeting.
quests.word: I'll bear that in mind.
quests.textToSpeak: I'll bear that in mind.
quests.hint: Does 'mind' land with energy, or just stop?
quests.explanation: Staying level and falling flat on 'mind' ends the exchange without any commitment. A genuine intention would lift on 'bear' and add a specific follow-up. A brush-off may leave the suggester believing they have been heard.
quests.meaningShift: A level, flat delivery is a polite brush-off; a lifted 'bear' with a follow-up would be genuine.

quests.instruction: A speaker is about to give a talk.
quests.word: I'd be lying if I said I wasn't nervous.
quests.textToSpeak: I'd be lying if I said I wasn't nervous.
quests.hint: Decide whether the voice rises at the end, as if asking.
quests.explanation: Falling steadily on 'nervous' with slightly lowered pitch shows the speaker simply sharing a feeling. Fishing for reassurance would lift at the end or on 'nervous' to invite a response. Listeners usually respond more warmly to the first.
quests.meaningShift: A steady, lowered fall is honest vulnerability; a lifted end would invite reassurance.
